changes.matn:
God created Ādam, taught him the names and entrusted humanity with a life on earth in which knowledge and obedience would be required. Ādam and his wife were given a place in the Garden and forbidden to approach a particular tree. When they disobeyed, they acknowledged their wrong and sought God's forgiveness. God accepted their repentance and sent them to earth with the promise of guidance. The account establishes at once the dignity of human knowledge, the reality of human error and the possibility of returning to God.

Nūḥ called his people to worship God and seek His forgiveness. He persisted in his preaching despite long resistance, addressing them openly and privately. Their leaders mocked him and disparaged those who followed him. When the flood came, Nūḥ built the Ark at God's command and called his son to embark. The son refused, trusting that a mountain would protect him, and was drowned. Nūḥ appealed to God concerning his son, and God clarified that the promise of deliverance did not extend to those who rejected His guidance. Nūḥ sought forgiveness for asking about what he did not know. His concern as a father was real, but kinship could not replace fidelity to God.

Hūd likewise called the people of ʿĀd to worship God alone. He challenged their pride in strength and impressive buildings and warned them against oppression. Ṣāliḥ addressed Thamūd, whose prosperity and carved dwellings did not free them from obedience to God. The she-camel was given to them as a sign, with an allotted share of water, but they violated the command concerning her. Neither power nor abundant provision could save a community determined to reject its messenger.

Lūṭ faced the people of his town when they threatened the guests who had come to him. He tried to protect them, while the visitors—angels sent by God—announced the approaching judgment and instructed him to depart with his household, except those excluded from deliverance. Shuʿayb called his people to worship God and to deal honestly in trade. He condemned the dishonest use of weights and measures and declared that he would not practise what he forbade others to do.

Ibrāhīm rejected idolatry and remained faithful to God despite opposition and difficult trials. He asked about the future of his descendants, and God made clear that His covenant did not extend to wrongdoers merely because of their descent. With Ismāʿīl, Ibrāhīm raised the foundations of the Sacred House and prayed for a community devoted to God. Ismāʿīl is remembered for keeping his promise and instructing his household in prayer and giving. Through Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb, guidance continued in other branches of the family.

Yūsuf was separated from his father by his brothers' betrayal, resisted temptation and was imprisoned before being vindicated. His interpretation of the ruler's dream led to measures for storing grain against years of famine. When his brothers came to Egypt, the story moved toward recognition, forgiveness and the reunion of a divided family. Mūsā grew up under a ruler who oppressed the Israelites. After leaving Egypt and living in Madyan, he received the divine call and was sent back to confront Pharaoh. The liberation of his people was followed by the harder work of keeping the covenant, worshipping faithfully and living together under God's guidance.

Dāwūd was given kingship, wisdom and the responsibility to judge justly; he is also remembered for praise of God and skilled work. Sulaymān received extensive rule and particular understanding, yet both kings remained answerable to the God who had granted their gifts.

Ayyūb endured severe affliction, prayed for relief and received healing. Yūnus called upon God in the darkness after leaving his people; God delivered him, and his people are remembered for repenting and being spared the threatened punishment. Zakariyyā prayed for a successor, and Yaḥyā was granted wisdom and tenderness. Maryam was sustained by God through extraordinary trials and gave birth to ʿĪsā, who called people to God and performed signs only by His permission.

The Qurʾān recounts these prophets not merely as figures of the past but as examples through which the final Messenger, Muḥammad ﷺ, and his community are instructed. Their missions unfolded among different peoples and circumstances, yet all called to worship of God and faithful action. The Prophet ﷺ received the final revelation and lived its guidance among his family, companions and wider community. His example would remain authoritative after his death, while later generations sought to understand and practise it in societies very different from the one in which he lived.
sharh_replacements: Nūḥ: rank, fidelity and the education of affection.
Nūḥ: worship, steadfastness and the claims of kinship.

Nūḥ’s opponents make social standing a criterion of truth. Their contempt for poor followers attempts to impose an existing hierarchy upon the reception of revelation. Refusing wages and refusing to expel believers belong together: the messenger does not bargain for acceptance through wealth or prestige. He answers to God for those whom the powerful would exclude.

Nūḥ's principal summons is clear in Sūrat Nūḥ (71:1–10): worship God, seek His forgiveness and heed His messenger. He speaks to his people over a long period, first openly and then privately, but their resistance persists. The chiefs' objection that only people of low standing have followed him (11:27–31; 26:111–115) is one aspect of that resistance. Nūḥ refuses to dismiss believing followers to satisfy the demands of the powerful. Their social rank cannot decide the truth of the message.

The Ark gives obedience a technical form. Instruction does not replace construction, and construction does not make the vessel an independent refuge. Preservation crosses the collapse of a social order without promising the survival of every relationship on its former terms. The paired creatures also admit an inward reading in which bodily and spiritual, sensible and intelligible, revealed law and realization must remain joined.

God commands Nūḥ to build the Ark (11:37–40), and he carries out the work while his opponents mock him. The vessel is a real means of rescue, but its construction and use occur under divine instruction. The Qurʾān then describes Nūḥ calling his son to board, the son's confidence that a mountain would protect him, and the flood that separates them (11:42–43). The son does not perish because Nūḥ loved him, but because he refused the guidance that had been offered.

The son’s loss tests more than ancestry. It brings paternal affection into a question about the scope of the divine promise. Nūḥ invokes both kinship and God’s unfailing word; the answer corrects his understanding of who belongs to the promised household. He seeks refuge from asking beyond his knowledge. The prophet who has taught his people now receives instruction in the adab of his own prayer.

Nūḥ's prayer after the drowning is especially delicate (11:45–47). He recalls that his son belongs to his family and that God's promise is true. God clarifies that the son is not among the family promised deliverance and warns Nūḥ against asking about what he does not know. Nūḥ immediately seeks divine forgiveness and mercy. Exegetes differ about what Nūḥ knew of his son's inward condition, and the readings of 11:46 are significant; the secure point is that biological descent does not entitle a person to salvation apart from faithful response to God.

This does not make affection a fault in itself. It specifies the relation between a genuine affection, the terms of a promise and the knowledge required to invoke it rightly. The narrative therefore links reception, social accountability, preservation and personal correction. The disputed Akbarian readings of the drowned people’s ultimate condition remain in the earlier dossier; they do not displace the Qurʾānic contrast between response and refusal.

The passage does not condemn a father's concern for his child. It distinguishes that concern from the authority of God's judgment, and it shows Nūḥ turning to God even after receiving correction. Some later Sufi and Akbarian commentaries explore the spiritual meanings of the flood and of those who drowned. Such interpretations must be attributed to their authors; they cannot reverse the Qurʾānic account of Nūḥ's summons, his son's refusal and God's answer.
Hūd and Shuʿayb: strength, worship and exchange.
Hūd and Shuʿayb: the call to worship and the demands of justice.

Hūd’s warning concerns a relation between monumental achievement, the imagination of permanence and coercive force. Architecture is not itself condemned. The transmitted meanings of *maṣāniʿ* include palaces, fortifications and waterworks; the term does not authorize one exact reconstruction of an ancient city. The narrative judges the purposes and pretensions attached to power rather than all durable construction.

Hūd calls ʿĀd to worship God and to abandon its arrogance. Qurʾān 26:128–130 refers to impressive constructions and the harsh exercise of power. The criticism falls upon boasting, oppression and the false security that people derive from strength, not upon building as such. Commentators offer different explanations of *maṣāniʿ*, including substantial buildings or works of water management; the passage does not identify one archaeologically verified site.

Shuʿayb’s opponents ask why his prayer should govern their inherited worship and use of property. Their objection separates devotion from the obligations of exchange. His reply joins them: reverence for the divine command requires care for those whom commercial acts affect. He also refuses to reserve for himself the practices he prohibits to others.

Shuʿayb's people question whether his prayer gives him grounds to challenge their worship and their use of wealth (11:87). He requires honest weights and measures, fair dealing and the abandonment of corruption. His answer (11:88) makes the demand personal: he will not do behind their backs what he has forbidden them to do. His trust in God is joined to a willingness to live by the guidance he proclaims.

The sign tests whether a society can limit its exercise of power without regarding that limitation as an intolerable affront. The episode prepares later questions about resource allocation, agreements and the public protection of vulnerable claims.

The she-camel's right to water is a concrete condition of the sign given to Thamūd. Their refusal illustrates how a prosperous community can reject the command of God when it conflicts with accustomed control of resources. The account can inform later reflection on shared rights, but its primary subject remains the people's response to their prophet.

Maryam supplies an explicit case. Provision first reaches her without ordinary effort; later she must shake the palm trunk. The spiritual interpretation preserved here treats the second condition as more complete: mature certainty permits the return to means. It rejects the explanation that motherhood necessarily divided her love and lowered her station.

Maryam receives provision without having to procure it in the account of her sanctuary (3:37). During childbirth she is instructed to shake the palm trunk so that dates fall to her (19:25). Later spiritual commentators have read this change as an education in reliance upon God while using ordinary means. The Qurʾān itself does not explicitly rank the two episodes as successive spiritual stations; that ranking belongs to interpretation.

**Link to the opening:** A comprehensive vocation requires knowledge of claims other than one's own. The sign tests whether a society can limit its exercise of power without regarding that limitation as an intolerable affront. The episode prepares later questions about resource allocation, agreements and the public protection of vulnerable claims.
The Qurʾānic account makes the people's treatment of the she-camel a test of obedience. Their use of water and the obligations attached to the divine sign become inseparable in their actual conduct.

matn_replacements: Humanity's earthly vocation unfolds through dependence upon created means.
Human life depends upon water, soil, plants, animals and the labour of other people.

These activities give practical expression to the Adamic capacity to understand the natures, properties and relations of things. They establish obligations because each person's livelihood depends upon the work, knowledge and restraint of others.
Such work requires observation, skill and cooperation. It also creates obligations among people whose livelihoods depend upon one another.
The same administrative knowledge that secured a worker's ration could determine what was taken from the farmer.
The records used to distribute food to workers could also be used to demand taxes and labour from farmers.

The prophets addressed human beings within such relationships, not outside them. Food, land, wealth, rank, kinship and political authority are genuine goods, but none determines its own proper limits.

The prophets addressed people who cultivated land, exchanged goods, raised families and lived under rulers. They taught that wealth, ancestry and political power did not release anyone from responsibility to God.
A community may possess powerful institutions without realizing their rightful ends, while a religious teaching may outlast the political arrangement that once supported it.

Powerful institutions could support worship and justice, but could also be used to oppress. Religious communities sometimes preserved their teaching after losing the kingdoms that had once protected them.
The covenant demanded fidelity in ordinary households as well as public life. A king could administer a territory; he could not make a people faithful simply by holding power.
Rulers and families alike remained responsible for their conduct. A kingdom could defend a sanctuary and administer justice, but political power alone could not secure fidelity to God.

A religious inheritance was capable of surviving political rupture, but its continuity required people who remembered, taught, interpreted and performed it. That difference between a revealed obligation and its changing political supports would recur throughout the later history of Islam.

Jewish religious life continued even where independent Jewish kingship had ended, sustained by families, teachers, communal worship and written traditions. Later Muslim communities would face related questions about preserving religious life under changing rulers, though the two histories followed different paths.
Moreover, a society's form of knowledge cannot be determined by treating an entire civilization as one spiritual station.
Each of these traditions developed through its own teachers, texts and social conditions.

The eventual Islamic encounter with philosophy, scripture and spiritual disciplines would arise from concrete transmissions through such communities, not from a single abstract awakening spanning Eurasia.

Muslims would later encounter these earlier traditions through specific texts, translations and communities of learning. Similar ideas across distant regions do not, by themselves, establish that those peoples had been in direct contact.

His healing and life-giving signs did not establish an independent source of divinity in the servant; they called witnesses to recognize the Giver and to direct their conduct accordingly. He taught persons whose ordinary relations of kin, property, obligation and public worship did not cease to matter.

The Qurʾān attributes his healing and life-giving signs to God's permission and presents them as signs of his mission. His call concerned the worship of God and the conduct of people in their daily lives.
When the Qurʾān addressed Christians, it spoke not to one undifferentiated philosophical formula but to actual communities with different histories, practices and authorities.

By the Prophet's lifetime, Christian communities near Arabia differed in language, worship and theological allegiance. The Qurʾānic engagement with Christians took place in a world where those differences mattered.
In the sixth century, Arabia lay among differentiated political and religious worlds.
In the sixth century, Arabia lay between several powerful states and religious communities.
The conditions under which one person could teach and another could receive instruction depended upon kin protection, economic standing and the willingness of others to listen.
Within the Ḥijāz, clan protection, household wealth and personal relationships shaped who could speak publicly and who could respond without fear.
The wars created conditions important for the later expansion of Muslim rule, but they cannot explain the divine origin of revelation.
The wars weakened the two empires before the later Muslim conquests. They do not explain the origin of the Prophet's revelation.
